input_text: Magnesium supplements improve sleep quality in older adults.

result.rule: The weighted evidence supports the claim.

quotes.label: supports
quotes.quote: There is minimal evidence of positive effect, of low to very low certainty, to suggest that magnesium supplementation improves insomnia symptoms as measured through sleep parameters.
quotes.reason: The passage reports minimal, low-certainty evidence that magnesium improves insomnia symptoms, with sleep-onset latency reduced versus placebo.
quotes.section: Results: Effect of intervention: Sleep parameters

quotes.label: supports
quotes.quote: Pooled analysis showed that post-intervention sleep onset latency time was 17.36 min less after magnesium supplementation compared to placebo (95% CI − 27.27 to − 7.44, p = 0.0006).
quotes.reason: The pooled analysis reports a statistically significant reduction in sleep onset latency with magnesium versus placebo, favouring the claimed sleep improvement.

quotes.label: supports
quotes.quote: Finally, earlier studies have shown that magnesium intake has a role in normalizing sleep organization, and its deficiency is linked to some sleep disturbances (25).
quotes.reason: The passage states that magnesium intake plays a role in normalizing sleep organization, which favours a sleep benefit, though it is background from earlier studies rather than a trial finding.

input_text: Beetroot juice improves endurance performance in cyclists.

result.rule: The weighted evidence contradicts the claim.

quotes.label: contradicts
quotes.quote: No significant effect of condition was observed for EP (p = 0.401, ηp2 = 0.056), WEP (p = 0.580, ηp2 = 0.048), peak power (p = 0.642, ηp2 = 0.046), mean power (p = 0.212, ηp2 = 0.108), or total work (p = 0.217, ηp2 = 0.107).
quotes.reason: The abstract reports no significant effect of beetroot juice (combined with caffeine condition) on end power, work above end power, peak or mean power in a 3 min all-out cycling test, which contradicts a performance benefit.

quotes.label: contradicts
quotes.quote: Collectively, these findings suggest that performance outcomes are not consistently improved across different supplementation conditions, although results remain dependent on the exercise model and population studied.
quotes.reason: The discussion summarises other studies, noting mixed and non-consistent performance outcomes from combined nitrate and caffeine, with no significant benefit in some, which argues against a consistent benefit.

quotes.label: contradicts
quotes.quote: Accordingly, the absence of an observed effect in the present study should be interpreted within the context of this potential mismatch between the physiological targets of nitrate supplementation and the characteristics of the exercise model.
quotes.reason: The discussion explains that the absence of nitrate effect in the 3MT may reflect a mismatch with the test, reporting no positive finding for beetroot juice on this claim.

quotes.label: supports
quotes.quote: TTE in BR+C was 46% higher than in PLA (P = 0.096) and 18% and 27% nonsignificant TTE improvements were observed on BR+C compared with BR and PLA+C alone, respectively.
quotes.reason: The abstract reports that beetroot juice plus caffeine improved time to exhaustion versus placebo, but the improvement was non-significant (P = 0.096) and the comparison was with caffeine, not a clear beetroot-alone endurance benefit in cyclists; it partly supports the claim.

quotes.label: supports
quotes.quote: Several independent research groups have demonstrated in double-blind, placebo-controlled studies that acute as well as chronic intake of beetroot juice containing about 8 mmoles of nitrate (NO3 −) can improve endurance and high-intensity intermittent performance [16–20].
quotes.reason: The introduction states that double-blind placebo-controlled studies show beetroot juice improves endurance performance, supporting the claim, though it is a literature summary rather than this study's finding.

quotes.label: supports
quotes.quote: acute consumption of beetroot juice resulted in improved 4 km and 16 km time trial performance in club-level competitive cyclists [19].
quotes.reason: The discussion reports that acute beetroot juice improved time trial performance in club-level cyclists, directly supporting the claim.

quotes.label: contradicts
quotes.quote: Further, Cermak et al. [31] found that consumption of a single dose of concentrated beetroot juice did not affect 1 h time-trial cycling exercise performance.
quotes.reason: The passage reports that a single dose of concentrated beetroot juice did not affect 1 h cycling time-trial performance, which contradicts the claim that beetroot juice improves endurance in cyclists.
